content.title: Artemis II crew splashes down, ending historic moon mission
content.text: 11:22 pm ET April 10, 2026NASA leaders jubilant, look toward future after Artemis II successAmanda Lee MyersNASA leaders declared victory after the Artemis II crew made a flawless splashdown back on Earth after a historic moon mission that will pave the way for humanity's return to the lunar surface in 2028."It’s good to be NASA, it’s good to be an American today," Shawn Quinn, exploration ground systems program manager, said at a news conference after the splashdown on Friday."Welcome to our moonshot," said Lori Glaze, deputy associate administrator of NASA’s Exploration Systems Development. "NASA has shown that ambitious goals are worth pursuing and can inspire the world."Rick Henfling, Artemis II entry flight director, quantified the success of the mission with a few telling numbers."Integrity and her crew of four astronauts flew 700,237 miles," he said. "We reached a peak velocity of 24,664 miles per hour. We hit our flight path angle target within .4 percent. We flew an entry range of 1,957 miles and we landed within less than a mile of our target. What a tremendous day."He spoke about the tense moments during and immediately after reentry, considered some of the most dangerous of the entire mission."We all breathed a sigh of relief once the side hatch opened up," he said. "We turned around to the families and waved to the families and gave them a thumbs up."The NASA leaders promised the world that much more is to come from its brave astronauts."Fifty three years ago humanity left the moon," said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator. "This time we return to stay. Let us finish what they started. Let us focus on what was left undone. Let us not go to plant flags and leave but to stay with firmness in our purpose."10:30 pm ET April 10, 2026Navy dive team assists Artemis II crewDinah Voyles PulverThe first faces on Earth the Artemis II crew saw on Friday were four U.S. Navy sailors on a dive medical, first contact team. The divers were there to open the capsule, checked the astronauts and assisted them out of the capsule.The team included Lt. Cmdr. Jesse Wang, Senior Chief Hospital Corpsman Laddy Aldridge, Chief Hospital Corpsman Vlad Link, and Hospital Corpsman 1st Class Steve Kapala, according to Fleet Forces Command. Aldridge, from Cushing, Oklahoma, was set to be the team member to open the capsule and begin medical assessments of the astronauts.Wang, the dive team lead, was heard on NASA's live feed as the team began communicating with the crew. “It is the honor of a lifetime to stand here today, ready to provide the absolute best care to the Artemis II crew,” he stated in a news release earlier on Friday.10:21 pm ET April 10, 2026Watch Artemis II astronauts exit OrionBrooke EdwardsMiss the action? Check out this video recap of the astronauts exiting the spacecraft after their journey around the moon.10:17 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II crew arrives on Naval shipAmanda Lee MyersThe Artemis II astronauts are back on solid ground. Sort of.Mission commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, crew specialist Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen are now on the USS John P. Murtha, the recovery ship for the Orion spacecraft.Once the U.S. Navy helped extract the astronauts from the Orion capsule, each one was hoisted into a helicopter. The helicopters then flew a short distance over to the ship.The astronauts were seen hanging out on the deck, looking relaxed and in good spirits as a photographer snapped photos. Koch waved to a NASA camera and punched her fists in the air in a sign of victory.Three U.S. Navy personnel helped each astronaut as they walked across the deck and to a medical bay, since they still need to get their Earth legs back in action. The crew members will be assessed their by their own nurses, get out of their clunky suits and confirm they're healthy after their long journey.9:58 pm ET April 10, 2026'You get that tear in your eye,' watching splashdownParis BarrazaMoments after splashdown, a tightly packed crowd inside the Pavilion of Flight at the San Diego Air & Space Museum chanted, "U.S.A."Hearing that chant, "you get that tear in your eye," said Larry Swan.The 57-year-old of Rancho Cucamonga, California, was there with his wife, Moe. He said being with a crowd to view the splashdown gave him "goosebumps." At least 100 people were waiting in line outside the museum less than an hour before the splashdown. Dozens of people inside the museum, near its information desk, sat on the floor in front of a smaller screen to watch the splashdown. Nearby, the museum's Pavilion of Flight was seemingly at capacity. Several people trying to enter the space were barred from where the larger viewing party was held. The Swans learned about the watch party on April 9, and said they'd rescheduled plans to be at the viewing party. "I want to be part of the history making," Moe Swan, 54, said. Carla Rodman, 70, of San Diego said she had no words when asked about how she felt watching the splashdown at the museum. "Every word that comes to me--awesome, amazing, super--none of them even touch the surface of the feeling that I have today," Rodman said. Rodman, her daughter and grandson have been following the Artemis II mission closely, she said. She said they've gotten to know the astronauts well through all the coverage of the mission. "It was the pinnacle to see them come back healthy, and they made it back alive," Rodman said.9:48 pm ET April 10, 2026Was there a sonic boom when Orion returned?Michael LoriaU.S. science officials have not confirmed whether NASA’s Orion returned to earth with a sonic boom, as expected.A sonic boom, the term for when an object moves faster than sound and creates a sound like thunder, was expected to be heard between 5 p.m. and 5:15 p.m. PT when the space capsule reentered the atmosphere. Officials at the U.S. Geological Survey expected the boom would "be felt and heard throughout Southern California."The geological agency asked people in the area of the capsule's reentry to report whether they heard or felt a boom.Geological agency officials did not immediately respond to requests for confirmation a sonic boom occurred.9:37 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II astronauts have left OrionAmanda Lee MyersThe four Artemis II astronauts have officially left the capsule.The astronauts left Orion around 6:30 p.m. PT with the help of a U.S. Navy extraction crew.The astronauts walked out of the capsule and onto a "front porch," a floating platform that connected to Orion, named "Integrity" by the crew.Meanwhile the mood at Mission Control was "raucous" as NASA celebrated the flawless splashdown and successful mission. NASA's livestream showed Mission Control cheering loudly as the first crew member came out of Integrity.The last crew member out was Commander Reid Wiseman.9:19 pm ET April 10, 2026Orion capsule is openAmanda Lee MyersThe Orion capsule has been opened for the four crew members on the Artemis II mission.U.S. Navy crews assessed the craft for any hazardous gases and cleared it before they opened the door.Four Navy personnel went inside the capsule, one to assess each astronaut individually. All eight remain inside.NASA is reporting that the four astronauts are “feeling great, happy to be home and ready to be extracted as soon as possible.”9:16 pm ET April 10, 2026'USA, USA!' Artemis II watch party erupts in cheersAmanda Lee MyersWatch as dozens of people burst into proud chants of "USA! USA!" just after the Artemis II crew safely splashed back down to Earth. The viewers were at a watch party in San Diego, California, where the splashdown happened.8:24 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II astronauts are 'hale and hearty'Amanda Lee MyersThe four Artemis II astronauts are back on Earth and "hale and hearty," according to NASA's livestream of the crew's incredible splashdown.It was "a perfect bulls-eye splashdown," the NASA narrator said on the livestream of the event that attracted more than 3 million viewers."What a journey," Commander Reid Wiseman said as he and the crew bobbed in the Pacific Ocean inside the Orion capsule.He reported that there were "four green crewmembers" inside, which means they were all safe and doing well.The splashdown off the coast of San Diego happened at 8:07 p.m. EDT / 5:07 PDT.8:08 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II crew splashes down, ending historic 10-day missionThe Orion spacecraft has splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, ending Artemis II’s historic 10-day mission to the moon and back.7:54 pm ET April 10, 2026Astronauts have begun reentryAmanda Lee MyersThe Artemis II astronauts have begun reentry into Earth's atmosphere.The capsule began maneuvering about 75 miles above the Earth for its final descent back to the surface. The spacecraft, moving at speeds up to 25,000 mph, is building up heat by creating shock waves. Those waves compress and superheat gas in the atmosphere to temperatures of 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit or more.Within seconds, superheated charged particles known as plasma build up around the spacecraft, causing a short communications blackout.The vehicle will ultimately deploy parachutes to make a water landing on the West Coast, where recovery teams will airlift the astronauts to a U.S. Navy vessel and transport them to shore.7:34 pm ET April 10, 2026Orion capsule separates in critical stepAmanda Lee MyersIn a critical step of the Artemis II splashdown process, the Orion capsule has successfully separated from the European Service Module.After the separation comes the burn that will bring the astronauts home. The splashdown is set for 8:07 p.m. ET.7:28 pm ET April 10, 2026Will dolphins greet Orion after splashdown?Dinah Voyles PulverCurious dolphins have been occasional visitors during other recent splashdown events when astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station.When NASA's Suni Williams and Butch Wilmore arrived off the west coast of Florida aboard the SpaceX Dragon capsule Freedom in March 2025, a pod of dolphins swam over. NASA's Johnson Space Center called them "the unplanned welcome crew!"Several dolphins also appeared in the water off the coast of California shortly after four astronauts returned early from the ISS in a Dragon capsule on Jan. 15.It remains to be seen if they'll appear during this splashdown, thought to be more than 50 miles offshore, but dolphins are commonly seen during whale watching cruises in the region off the California coast near San Diego and La Jolla. A super pod with thousands of dolphinswas seen in March 2025.7:19 pm ET April 10, 2026California museum hosts Artemis II splashdown watch partyParis BarrazaFive hundred people signed up in advance to attend a watch party at the San Diego Air & Space Museum as the historic Artemis II mission, which set a new record for human spaceflight, nears its end.The museum, located at Balboa Park, is throwing a family pajama party as astronauts make a water landing off San Diego’s coast on Friday. David Neville, communications director, anticipated it’ll be standing room only as it gets closer to splashdown.“This is probably the most exciting thing this museum has ever done,” Neville said. “It’s definitely the most exciting thing I’ve done since I’ve been here… this is so anticipated. People all around the world have looked at the Artemis II program and have said, ‘How exciting is this. We went back to the moon.’”Dozens of people had gathered at the museum’s Pavilion of Flight as of 3 p.m. PDT on Friday — an hour before the viewing party officially began.Among the attendees is Brenna Ring, 65, of La Mesa, California. She will be joined by her two sisters for the watch party.“I’m going to cry, I know, when they land,” Ring said. “I think that’s what I’ll do.”7:01 pm ET April 10, 2026How survival suits protect Artemis II crewAmanda Lee MyersThe bulky orange space suits that the Artemis II crew astronauts are wearing as they prepare for splashdown on Earth are specially designed to protect them. They help the astronauts maintain blood pressure and circulation during their transition back to Earth's gravity, NASA says.NASA says the so-called Orion Crew Survival System suits also can provide life support in the event of cabin depressurization and survival operations after splashdown."After extended time in microgravity, some astronauts experience orthostatic intolerance, a condition that can make it difficult to stand upright without dizziness or fainting," NASA says. "The garment applies lower‑body compression to counteract this effect and support a safe return."6:52 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II reentry risk explainedDinah Voyles PulverThis evening's reentry is considered one of the more dangerous parts of the entire Artemis II mission. That’s because of the atmosphere that surrounds and protects the Earth. Remember all those pockmarks on the lunar surface this week? The atmosphere helps protect us from much of the activity that causes those craters on the moon. NASA calls it our planet’s security blanket.But it's rough on returning spacecraft. Orion will begin to experience its effects while still nearly 76 miles above the Earth. That’s when “superheated plasma” will begin to build around the capsule, friction increases and temperatures on the exterior could reach more than 3,000 degrees.Orion's heat shield protection system "will bear the full force of that reentry," NASA official Amit Kshatriya said in an April 9 news conference.Questions about the heat shield arose after external damage appeared when the unpiloted Artemis I returned to Earth in 2022. The issue was flagged in a post-flight Inspector General’s report and NASA has said it has worked to address the issue. NASA has “high confidence in the system, in the heat shield and parachutes and recovery systems we put together.”Today’s re-entry is the first live test of those changes, according to a April 10 post by Northeastern University. Jacqueline McCleary, an assistant professor of physics at the school, said “scientists don’t actually know what the odds of failure are." But she added, she would be confident riding in the capsule.5:11 pm ET April 10, 2026What's next? NASA targets 2027 for Artemis III test missionEric LagattaNASA's next mission under the Artemis program is slated to get off the ground sometime in 2027.Preparations for Artemis III are already underway before the Artemis II mission is even back on the ground. NASA is preparing to roll out and transport to Florida a new core stage for the gigantic 322-foot Space Launch System rocket that would help launch the mission.The Artemis III mission will send a new crew of astronauts on the Orion spacecraft to Earth's orbit. There, they will dock with at least one of the commercial lunar landers being developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin.NASA will also use the mission to test space suits, known as extravehicular activity suits, being developed by Axiom Space for astronauts on the lunar surface.4:38 pm ET April 10, 2026Why the Pacific off San Diego for Artemis' reentry?Dinah Voyles PulverNASA didn’t just look at the idyllic waters off the Southern California coast and randomly choose a location for the Orion capsule to return to Earth. Far from it. A lot of very complex calculus and physics went into the determination.These formulas take into account the approach from the moon, entry angle, speed and thermal limits. One early NASA planning document explained how it targeted longitudes in the region based on the Earth’s atmosphere and where it’s slightly more flat than others. According to NASA documents, the location also provides some limited space for a flight diversion if a storm arose.It does make it a little easier that the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego has a reputation for being a bit calmer. In general that region of the ocean is less exposed to extreme conditions, in part because of a cold current that tends to limit extreme weather variations compared to some other locations. And thanks in part to the region's kelp forests and university researchers, it’s been called one of the most studied ocean areas in the world.3:53 pm ET April 10, 2026Where is Artemis II? 35,000 miles from EarthDoyle RiceAs of 3:30 p.m. EDT, "the Artemis II crew is now under 35,000 miles from Earth," according to a NASA post on X."The astronauts are preparing the spacecraft for reentry and the weather is looking good for splashdown."3:19 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II splashdown timelineDoyle RiceA carefully timed sequence will guide Orion through the final stages of descent (all times are EDT):7:33 p.m.: Orion’s crew module will separate from the service module, exposing its heat shield for the spacecraft’s return through Earth’s atmosphere, where it will encounter temperatures of about 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit.7:37 p.m.:Following separation, Orion will perform an 18-second crew module raise burn, beginning to set the proper entry angle and align the heat shield for atmospheric interface.7:53 p.m.:Orion reaches 400,000 feet above Earth’s surface while traveling nearly 35 times the speed of sound. The crew is expected to experience up to 3.9 Gs. This moment marks the spacecraft’s first contact with the upper atmosphere and the start of a planned 6-minute communications blackout as plasma builds around the capsule.8:03 p.m.: Around 22,000 feet in altitude, the drogue parachutes will deploy, slowing and stabilizing the capsule as Orion nears splashdown.8:04 p.m.: At around 6,000 feet, the drogues will release and the three main parachutes will deploy, reducing Orion’s speed to less than 136 mph.8:07 p.m.: Slowing to 20 mph, Orion will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, completing the Artemis II crew’s return to Earth and a 694,481-mile journey.2:38 pm ET April 10, 2026Final return burn sets Orion for homeDoyle RiceNASA reports that Orion's third return burn will occur at 2:53 p.m. EDT, refining its path for atmospheric entry and splashdown. During the maneuver, the spacecraft will make precise adjustments to stay on its targeted course home.2:09 pm ET April 10, 2026USS John P. Murtha to recover Artemis II astronauts following splashdownDoyle RiceThe U.S. Navy ship USS John P. Murtha has begun positioning itself for the Artemis II splashdown around 50 nautical miles off the coast of San Diego.Here are a few details about the recovery, all from NASA:The ship will be positioned approximately 1.5-2 miles from the splashdown point.After initial positioning, the ship will circle the capsule, so the port (left) side faces the capsule.Divers will conduct a hazard assessment in the water before opening the capsule hatch.Once cleared, divers will open the hatch, and Navy medical staff will perform initial checks on the astronauts, determining whether anyone requires priority transport back to the ship.Two Navy Seahawk MH-60 helicopters will transport the astronauts back to the ship one at a time.If all goes well, NASA plans to have the full crew aboard within 1-2 hours of splashdown.Following medical checks, the astronauts will depart the ship by air, returning to San Diego and then onward to Houston.Recovering the capsule can take several additional hours, often 4-6 hours after splashdown, and sometimes longer.1:30 pm ET April 10, 2026Sonic boom expected as spacecraft reenters Earth's atmosphereDoyle Rice and Natalie Neysa AlundA sonic boom is expected as the Artemis II mission's Orion spacecraft reenters the atmosphere during its return to Earth, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).The thunderous sound will likely take place between 5 p.m. and 5:15 p.m. Pacific Time, the USGS wrote in a post on X.The boom, USGS said, may be heard throughout Southern California.1:13 pm ET April 10, 2026Weather looks 'favorable' for Artemis II splashdownDoyle RiceThe weather forecast remains favorable for a safe splashdown in the Pacific on Friday evening, according to meteorologists from AccuWeather."The forecast is trending in the right direction for splashdown," said AccuWeather meteorologist Heather Zehr in an email to USA TODAY. "The rain threat has diminished, seas remain manageable, and conditions look favorable for Artemis II to make a smooth return to Earth.”“A storm affecting northern and central California is expected to stay far enough away to keep the splashdown zone dry during the key window," she added. "Winds below 15 mph and waves of 3 to 5 feet should be manageable for both splashdown and recovery. Air and water temperatures will be in the low to mid-60s.”12:43 pm ET April 10, 2026Where will Artemis II land?Doyle RiceThe four astronauts will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California.12:30 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II reentry speed estimated at 25,000 mphDoyle RiceWhen they enter Earth's atmosphere, the astronauts in the Orion capsule will be moving at an estimated 25,000 mph, which will rival the fastest speed ever experienced by humans. A series of parachutes will deploy to eventually slow them down to 17 mph ahead of the water landing.A heat shield will protect them from an estimated 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit.The astronauts will experience an estimated 3.9 Gs.12:30 pm ET April 10, 2026When is splashdown for Artemis II?Doyle RiceThe Orion capsule is due to reenter Earth's atmosphere today, April 10, splashing down off the coast of California at 8:07 p.m. EDT.
